levels.title: Qualifying, declining and re-deciding: disciplined decisions before and after an application

units.title: Qualifying a prospect honestly: screening, declines and re-applying

lessons.title: Pre-application qualification as a two-sided screen
lessons.explanation: A pre-application screen asks two questions in the same breath: is this file fundable by anyone in the network we actually have, and is applying now in this merchant's interest? Most training material only asks the first. The second is where the merchant's money is. A screen is not an application. No signed application, no credit inquiry, no fee, no commitment — just a structured conversation plus whatever evidence the merchant already has in hand. Establish eight facts before anything is submitted. First, who the legal applicant is: entity type, ownership percentages, and who has authority to sign. Second, how long the business has been operating and whether it has an existing stream of receivables the product can reach, because a purchase of receivables needs receipts to purchase. Third, the specific use the money serves and when that use actually occurs; a use dated six weeks out and a schedule starting tomorrow are incompatible. Fourth, the amount the business can service, which is not the amount it wants — compute headroom from deposits minus every existing debit, not from gross revenue. Fifth, every existing obligation with its payment, frequency, remaining balance and payoff figure, plus any filed lien. Sixth, whether a personal guarantee will be required and who will give it. Seventh, the conditions that disqualify a file at every funder regardless of who submits it: an illegal activity, a revenue base that is more than one third legal gambling, a pyramid plan, an associate under indictment or on probation for a financial crime, an owner without capacity to contract. Eighth, whether the merchant has understood the cost in dollars per hundred dollars of net proceeds and the total repayment amount, not a factor alone. If we cannot say the file is fundable on the evidence in front of us, we say that plainly. A screen that ends in “not with what we have” is a completed, useful piece of work; a screen that ends in an application we knew would fail is a cost we transferred to the merchant.
lessons.example: Halbrook Hardware asks for $60,000. The owner has 14 months of operating history, roughly $612,000 in annual card and bank deposits, three of the twelve statement months we requested, two open advances with $27,000 and $9,000 remaining and nine and six weeks left respectively, and an unsatisfied $11,400 judgment from a supplier dispute that the owner believes was resolved. The screen takes one and a half hours and produces three conclusions. First, the unsatisfied judgment plus the two open obligations place the file below the fundable line for every product we can place, so an application now ends in a decline on a file the funder can see is incomplete. Second, even if the judgment were satisfied tomorrow, the combined remaining obligations of $36,000 against the deposits shown leave about $2,240 of weekly headroom after a 40 percent contribution margin, which supports a materially smaller advance than the requested $60,000. Third, the merchant should be told what would change the answer. Now price the two paths. The unscreened path consumed nine hours of the owner's time and attention; at an opportunity cost of $45 an hour that is $405. Ten statement reprints at $5 each is $50, and a third-party processing fee of $1,500 is non-refundable in this illustration. The customer's total exposure on a file that cannot fund is $405 + $50 + $1,500 = $1,955. The screened path costs 1.5 hours × $45 = $67.50. The saving is $1,955 − $67.50 = $1,887.50, which is 96.55 percent of the unscreened cost. Now the part that has to be said out loud: on a $60,000 advance at a three percent commission the advisor would earn $1,800 if it funded. That $1,800 is 92.07 percent of the merchant's $1,955 loss on the failed path. The advisor's downside is zero and the merchant's is $1,955. That asymmetry is why the screen must be written down and shown to the merchant rather than performed silently in the advisor's head.
lessons.question: A merchant with two open advances and an unsatisfied judgment asks you to submit an application today for $60,000, “because a no costs nothing.” What is the defensible response?
lessons.answer: Decline to submit today, write a dated screen note naming the judgment and the combined obligations as the blocking conditions, and offer a verification plan with the documents and payoff figures that would change the answer.
lessons.distractor: Submit the application anyway because the merchant asked for it, and let the funder's decline settle the question at no cost to anyone.
lessons.correction: The decline is not free. In the worked figures the merchant spends $1,955 in time, statement fees and a non-refundable processing fee for a file that cannot fund, while the advisor risks nothing and stands to earn $1,800 if it somehow lands. Submitting a known-unfundable file transfers cost to the party with less information. A screen note plus a verification plan delivers the same “no” while preserving the merchant's money and the option to return with a fundable file.

depth.definitions: Prequalification is a non-binding assessment based on information the merchant states or on data the merchant supplies and controls; it creates no obligation and should involve no inquiry that affects credit standing. An application is a request for credit or for the purchase of receivables made under the funder's terms, and it starts clocks and obligations. A disqualifier is a condition that bars a program regardless of the strength of the file, such as an ineligible business type. An affordability condition is a measured gap between what the business can service and what it is asking for. A blocking document is evidence without which no decision can be made: payoff letters, a UCC search, ownership documents. File completeness is the share of the required inventory actually present with a source and a date. Headroom is deposits less every existing debit, after a stated contribution margin. The screen is two-sided because fundability answers the funder's question and timing answers the merchant's.
depth.mechanism: Screening works because an application is not a decision point but the entry to a chain: submission, then document verification, then underwriting, then notification, then funding. A file that enters the chain without its evidence does not receive a considered credit decision; it receives a documentation-driven outcome, usually a decline for insufficiency, which is both wasteful and information-losing, because a decline on an incomplete file teaches the merchant nothing about what to fix. A decline on a verified file with a stated reason does. The screen deliberately moves the evidence check ahead of the entry point so that the eventual decision, whatever it is, is about the business rather than about the paperwork. There is a second mechanism at work, and it is arithmetic rather than procedural: the merchant bears the time, the fees and the opportunity cost of a failed attempt, while the advisor's compensation is conditional on a funded transaction and therefore is zero on the failed path. When the party with the weaker information also bears the larger cost, the advisor has an obligation to make the screen explicit and auditable rather than to let the market structure speak for itself.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting file screens in but should still be deferred, which is the case most advisors get wrong. A six-year-old bakery with $910,000 in annual deposits, clean obligations and a $1,400 weekly headroom after existing debits asks for $80,000 in the second week of October to buy November and December inventory. Nothing in the file is disqualifying, and an unsophisticated screen would pass it straight through. The timing is the problem: a fixed 26-week schedule beginning in October carries the largest remittances through the bakery's two strongest months and then continues through the January–February trough, when deposits in this illustration run 26 percent below the annual average. The screen's conclusion is not “decline” and not “apply today”. It is that the file is fundable, the requested structure is not, and the options in order of preference are: a share-of-receipts structure that falls with sales, a shorter term with a sized-down amount, or an application in January when the trough is measurable rather than projected. Same file, same fundability, a different answer because the screen asked the second question too.
depth.mistake: The most common error is the belief that asking for the maximum and letting the funder decline is costless market discovery. The correction is to make the cost visible before the attempt: name the hours, the fees and the non-refundable items, and compare them with the cost of a screen. A related mistake is treating the number of applications as evidence of effort; in this market multiple simultaneous submissions create competing obligations, repeated inquiries and, in some files, an obligation count that itself becomes the reason for decline. The diagnostic question for a learner is: “What did the merchant learn, and what did it cost, from the last attempt?” If the answer is “nothing, and $1,955”, the screen was skipped.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: take a merchant you know only from conversation and write a one-page screen with three sections — established facts with sources, blocking conditions with the evidence that would clear each, and open questions with who can answer them. Then score your own screen: does every fact carry a source and a date; does every blocking condition name a measurable threshold; does the note state the two-sided conclusion (fundable or not, now or later)? Model response: a strong screen names at least one condition that is permanent, one that is fixable within ninety days, and one that is documentation-only, and it states the amount the evidence supports rather than the amount requested. Self-review rubric: a screen without sources is a sales note, not a screen; a screen without a two-sided conclusion has answered only the funder's question.
depth.summary: Screening is the point at which the advisor's duty and the funder's interest are most likely to diverge, so it must be documented rather than assumed. The screen establishes identity, tenure, use and timing, serviceable amount, obligations, guarantee requirements, permanent disqualifiers and cost comprehension — then states two conclusions instead of one. The transferable habit is to price the attempt before making it: hours multiplied by opportunity cost, plus fees, plus the non-refundable items, compared with the cost of a structured hour or two of review. On the figures used here the screen was 96.55 percent cheaper than the failed attempt, and the advisor's forgone commission was 92.07 percent of the merchant's loss. Those two numbers are the argument.

visual.title: The two-sided screen: fundability and timing checked in the same pass
visual.description: A labeled sequence showing how one merchant conversation produces two separate conclusions and one written note, rather than an application submitted on hope.
steps: Column one — fundability: entity and ownership, tenure, revenue that the product can reach, permanent disqualifiers. Each line ends in pass, fail, or unknown with a source.

Column two — the merchant's interest: the dated use of funds, deposits less every existing debit to find headroom, the amount the evidence supports, and whether cost has been understood in dollars per hundred dollars of net.
Gate: if either column reads fail or unknown, the output is a written screen note naming the blocking condition and the evidence that would clear it — not an application.
If both columns pass, the next step is a named product and a named structure, with the schedule's start date matched to the date the money is actually used.
Ledger line at the foot of the note: hours × opportunity cost, statement and processing fees, and any non-refundable amount, so the cost of the attempt is on the page before the attempt is made.

lessons.title: Disqualifying conditions versus fixable conditions: the “not yet” answer
lessons.explanation: A decline and a deferral are different products, and merchants are usually handed the wrong one. A disqualifying condition bars a program regardless of how strong everything else is: a business engaged in activity that is illegal under federal, state or local law; a revenue base deriving more than one third of gross annual revenue from legal gambling; a pyramid sale distribution plan; a life insurance company; a non-profit, with for-profit subsidiaries excepted; a passive business owned by a developer or landlord that does not occupy the assets financed; a loan packager earning more than one third of gross annual revenue from packaging. Some of those are permanent features of the entity and some are statuses that time resolves. A fixable condition is a gap that closes with a payment, a filing, a document or a date: an unsatisfied judgment that can be paid and released; a tax lien with a stated payoff; a collection account that is disputed and awaiting the reporting agency's reinvestigation; a missing payoff letter; a debt schedule that understates an obligation. A documentation-only condition closes without any change in the business at all — a UCC search, tax transcripts, ownership documents, a lease. The discipline this lesson installs is classification: every blocking condition on a file goes into one of three columns, and each column carries a different message. Permanent means the product is wrong or the business is out of scope, and the honest answer is no. Status-based means wait for a date or a status change. Fixable means here is the amount, the payee and the expected clearance time. Documentation-only means here is the request list. This is the substance behind the phrase “not yet”, which is only honest when it is followed by a measurable condition. “Not yet” with no condition attached is a soft decline wearing better manners, and it wastes the merchant's remaining patience.
lessons.example: Delgado Print & Sign presents a file with nine blocking issues. Classify them. Permanent-for-this-entity: the applicant is a non-profit trade association seeking funds for its own operations; more than one third of the revenue came from a licensed gaming room attached to the building; the business leases its equipment to a third party and does not operate it. Status-based, resolves with time or a change of status: a minority owner is the subject of a pending indictment for a financial offence and the business has an Associate in that position; a $6,400 state tax lien is on file and payable. Fixable with money or a filing: an unsatisfied $14,600 judgment the owner has already agreed to pay; a prior advance with a payoff figure that has not been obtained. Documentation-only: no UCC or lien search has been run; no tax transcripts have been ordered; ownership documents are missing for two of four owners. The owner's own first pass had classified five of the nine correctly, which is 55.56 percent — useful context for how poorly this skill is usually performed without a framework. Now attach time to the two that matter. The $14,600 judgment at a negotiated $1,080 per week takes 13.52 weeks, so fourteen weeks in practice, before the file can be re-presented. The $6,400 lien at $800 a month takes eight months. Those are the two numbers in the whole conversation that the merchant can act on. The verdict is not “no”. The verdict is: this file needs fourteen weeks for the judgment and would still fail on the gaming revenue share, which is a structural condition that cannot be timed away while that revenue line exists. Written that way, the merchant knows exactly which of the two problems is worth solving and which one means the product is simply wrong.
lessons.question: A merchant has an unsatisfied $14,600 judgment she is already paying down, a $6,400 tax lien, no UCC search on file and no tax transcripts ordered. Which response is the honest one?
lessons.answer: “Not yet” with named conditions: the judgment at $1,080 a week clears in fourteen weeks, the UCC search and transcripts are documentation-only items we can order this week, and the lien is a separate eight-month item at $800 a month.
lessons.distractor: “Not now — come back in a few months when your credit looks better”, which leaves the merchant with no idea which item controls or how long it takes.
lessons.correction: The second answer sounds kinder and is less useful. A deferral without a named condition, an amount, a payee and a clearance time cannot be acted on, and the merchant will spend the next three months applying elsewhere with the same file and the same result. The conditions, not the tone, are what makes a deferral honest. Note also that two items here are documentation-only and should not defer anything: a UCC search and tax transcripts change what we know, not what the business is.

depth.definitions: A disqualifying condition is a bar to a program that other file strengths cannot overcome, such as an ineligible business type or an Associate with a disqualifying criminal status. A fixable condition is a measured deficit that a payment, filing or document can close. A documentation-only condition is an evidence gap that closes with no change in the business. Clearance time is the interval between today and the date a condition is expected to satisfy the funder's requirement. Re-presentation is the date on which a deferred file can be considered again with the same evidence standard. Structural versus temporal distinguishes a condition inherent in the business model from one that exists only until a status or a balance changes.
depth.mechanism: The classification matters because the three columns route to different actions and only one of them is about the merchant trying harder. A documentation-only gap is the advisor's work: order the search, request the transcripts, obtain the schedule. A fixable gap is a payment plan against a named balance, and its only useful outputs are an amount, a payee and a date. A permanent disqualifier is a routing decision: the product or the program is wrong, and no amount of documentation or waiting changes the eligibility rule. A status-based disqualifier is the only one where the answer genuinely is time, and even then the time is bounded by a specific event — a probation terminating, an indictment resolving, a sold revenue line ending — not by a vague improvement in a credit score. The failure mode the framework prevents is the blended answer, in which a permanent disqualifier is described as a fixable one so that a sale remains theoretically alive. That description is not optimism; it is a misstatement about eligibility, and the merchant will act on it by spending money.
depth.secondExample: The mirror-image case shows why classification also guards against overdeclining. A wholesaler of restaurant equipment has two items that look alarming on a first read: a $22,000 judgment and a prior advance the merchant mentioned in a hallway. Both land in the fixable column once examined. The judgment was entered five years ago against a similarly named entity that is not the applicant, and a search of the docket shows the case was dismissed against the correct defendant; the fix is a certified copy of the dismissal, a documentation item, not a payment. The prior advance was paid off eleven weeks earlier; the attached search shows the financing statement is still of record, which is a real problem of a different kind, because an unsatisfied filing of record affects priority until a termination statement is filed. Note the mechanism: under Article 9 a filing remains effective for five years and is not automatically removed when the obligation ends; the secured party's obligation to send a termination statement runs from an authenticated demand from the debtor, and the statutory period for compliance is twenty days. The action item belongs to the merchant and is a written demand, not a payment. Two conditions that looked fatal cost one certified copy and one demand letter.
depth.mistake: The recurring misconception is that a deferral is a face-saving decline and that merchants prefer it. Merchants prefer specificity. The diagnostic test is to read your own deferral back and ask whether a stranger could act on it: can they identify the condition, compute the money, name the payee, and put a date on the calendar? If any of those four is missing, the deferral is a decline with extra words. A second error is classifying on the basis of difficulty rather than eligibility. A condition is permanent because the rule says so, not because it would be hard to fix; and it is fixable because a payment or document closes it, not because the merchant is likeable.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: take a real or constructed file with at least six blocking items and sort them into the three columns, then write the one-paragraph message you would send. Model response: the paragraph names each permanent disqualifier as a routing statement, each fixable condition with amount, payee and clearance date, and each documentation item with who will produce it and by when; it ends with a single re-presentation date. Self-review rubric: a correct answer has no condition in two columns at once, no condition without a source, and no “come back in a few months” phrasing anywhere in it.
depth.summary: Eligibility rules are categorical while files feel continuous, and the advisor's job is to translate between them without blurring either. Three columns — permanent, fixable, documentation-only — with status-based conditions sitting inside the fixable column as cases in which the fix is a date. The transferable skill is turning “not yet” into a sentence with an amount, a payee and a calendar date, while saying plainly when no date will help because the eligibility rule itself excludes the business. The 55.56 percent classification result in the worked example is a reminder that this is a trained skill, not an instinct.

visual.title: Three-column classification of every blocking condition on a file
visual.description: A labeled decision diagram that routes each blocking item to a permanent, fixable or documentation-only column, and attaches an owner and a date to the two columns that can move.
steps: Column A — permanent for this entity: illegal activity, gaming revenue above one third, pyramid plan, passive lessor that does not occupy the assets, non-profit applicant. Output: a routing statement, and the honest answer is no.

Column B — fixable: a named balance, a payee, a payment amount and a clearance date. Status-based conditions enter here too, with the triggering event written as the date rather than a credit-score hope.
Column C — documentation-only: UCC and lien searches, tax transcripts, ownership documents, payoff figures. Owner is the advisor or the merchant, and no payment is involved.
Merge line: conditions in B and C are listed together in the merchant message with amounts and dates; conditions in A are listed separately as eligibility bars that no date will resolve.
Final cell: one re-presentation date, computed from the longest live clearance time, so the deferral ends in a calendar entry rather than an intention.

lessons.title: Explaining a decline honestly and usefully: notification, reasons and what a broker may not say
lessons.explanation: Most declines are delivered badly, and the delivery is usually where the merchant loses the most. Three different declines get collapsed into one sentence. There is the funder's decline, which carries legal content: under Regulation B the creditor must notify the applicant of action taken, and for a business that had gross revenues of $1 million or less in its preceding fiscal year the creditor must comply with the ordinary notification rules — with a written statement of specific reasons, or a disclosure of the right to request one, and the ECOA notice. For a business above $1 million in gross revenues, or for trade credit, credit incident to a factoring agreement or similar business credit, the creditor must notify the applicant within a reasonable time, orally or in writing, of the action taken, and must provide a written statement of reasons only if the applicant makes a written request within sixty days of that notification. There is the advisor's own decline, which is not a legal event at all but a judgement that the file does not fit the products available, and which deserves to be stated as such. And there is the servicer's or platform's decline, which frequently arrives as a status change in a portal with no reason attached. The specific-reasons requirement has teeth: a statement that the action was based on internal standards or policies, or that the applicant failed to achieve a qualifying score on the creditor's scoring system, is expressly insufficient. That single sentence is the most useful line in the regulation for a merchant, because it tells the merchant that “internal criteria” is not a reason. A broker explaining a decline must therefore do four things: identify whose decision it is, state the reason as the funder gave it without embellishment, distinguish what is verifiable from what is speculation, and say plainly what the merchant can and cannot act on. What a broker may not do is narrower and clearer: never guarantee that a future application will be approved, never imply special influence or an affiliation with a government agency, never promise a fee that does not bear a reasonable relationship to work actually performed, and never state a reason the funder did not give.
lessons.example: Marisol Robles applies on 3 March 2026 for $45,000 for a second food truck. She supplies bank statements, a lease for the commissary, a personal financial statement and a processor report. The application is complete on the date it is submitted. On 2 April, thirty days later, the funder declines and sends a letter whose entire stated reason is that the applicant “did not meet our internal credit criteria.” Two problems with that and one with what happens next. First, check the clock: notification is due within thirty days after receiving a completed application for approval, counteroffer or adverse action, so 3 March plus thirty days is 2 April, and the notice is timely. Second, check the content: for a business at or below $1 million in gross revenue the applicant is entitled to a statement of specific reasons, and the letter offered none — it gave a restatement of internal standards, which the regulation identifies as insufficient. The advisor's correct action is to tell the merchant in writing that she may request a statement of specific reasons within sixty days of the notification, which puts the request deadline at 1 June 2026, and to give her the name, address and telephone number of the office that can supply it. Now the cost of not doing that. Suppose instead the advisor simply reports “you were declined, try these two other funders” and the merchant applies to both immediately. Each application costs $50 in document and statement fees and two hours of her time at $45 an hour, so $140 each, and the pair costs $280 — $420 in total across the three attempts including the original — plus six hours of her week, all without ever learning why the first one declined. The specific-reason route costs one written request and produces a sentence she can act on. Those two outcomes are not close.
lessons.question: A funder declines a merchant's application with the written reason “did not meet our internal credit criteria.” The merchant is a $640,000-revenue business. What should you tell her?
lessons.answer: That the stated reason is not a specific reason under Regulation B, that she may request a statement of specific reasons in writing within sixty days of the notification, and that the request goes to the named office on the notice — then hold further applications until the reason is known.
lessons.distractor: That “internal criteria” means the credit score was too low, and that the fastest route is to apply to two other funders immediately while the file is warm.
lessons.correction: The advisor cannot know what internal criteria meant, and inventing a credit-score explanation is a misstatement about the reason for a decline. The regulation treats a restatement of internal standards, or a bare reference to a qualifying score, as an insufficient statement of reasons — so the correct move is to tell her how to obtain the real one. Filing two more applications before the reason is known spends about $420 and six hours of her week to obtain information she is entitled to for the price of a letter.

depth.definitions: Action taken means approval, counteroffer or adverse action. Notification is the creditor's required communication of that action, with content and timing set by Regulation B. A statement of specific reasons must identify the principal reason or reasons and may not consist of a reference to internal standards, policies or a qualifying score. The ECOA notice is the prescribed statement of the Equal Credit Opportunity Act's prohibition on discrimination for inclusion with adverse action notification. A written-request threshold applies to larger businesses and to certain business credit: above $1 million in preceding-fiscal-year gross revenues, or trade credit, credit incident to a factoring agreement or similar business credit, the creditor must give reasons in writing only on the applicant's written request within sixty days. Third-party submission covers applications made on the applicant's behalf, including through a broker, and permits the creditor to notify through that party provided the notice identifies each creditor on whose behalf it is given.
depth.mechanism: The regulation's structure answers a question that a merchant naturally gets wrong: it assumes the decline is ours to explain. It is not. Notification duties run from creditor to applicant, and the content standard is deliberately calibrated so that the merchant receives something operational. The distinction between the two business-credit tracks is a real consequence of size and product type: below the $1 million revenue line and for ordinary business credit the creditor must notify of action taken and either give specific reasons or disclose the right to request them, while above that line and for trade or factoring-type credit the creditor may satisfy its obligation with a reasonable-time oral or written notice of the action and supply written reasons only on request. Knowing which track a file sits on is what stops an advisor from demanding reasons the funder does not owe and from overlooking reasons the funder does owe. Separately, the advisor's own conduct rules come from a different source: because a broker may not give a guaranty that an application will be approved, may not imply special influence, and may not charge fees without a reasonable relationship to services rendered, the explanatory conversation has to be honest about uncertainty. Saying “I don't know why yet, and here is how we find out” is compliant and useful; supplying a confident invented reason is neither.
depth.secondExample: The contrasting case is a decline the advisor owns rather than the funder. A landscaper asks for $70,000 in February to buy two trucks before the spring season. Nothing is disqualified and no document is missing, but deposits run $41,000 a month, existing obligations consume $2,100 a week, and a 32 percent contribution margin leaves $5,612 a week of contribution. The requested $70,000 at a factor of 1.35 over 26 weeks would take $3,634.62 a week, which is 64.76 percent of contribution, and the combined load would make coverage 0.98 on the funder's own arithmetic. Here the advisor's message is not “the funder declined” at all: it is “I will not submit this structure, here is the arithmetic that shows why, and here is the amount the evidence supports.” That is a different letter with a different clock, and it should say so explicitly, because a merchant who believes a funder has judged them behaves differently from one who understands that a size was wrong. The same file at $45,000 over 26 weeks is $2,336.54 a week and 41.63 percent of contribution, which is a structure worth presenting, with coverage of 1.27.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is substituting the advisor's guess for the funder's reason: the merchant is told the score was too low, or that the file lacked a year of history, when the funder said nothing of the kind. The diagnostic correction is a two-question test before any explanation is spoken: what exact words did the funder use, and can I produce the document that contains them? If the second answer is no, the explanation must be phrased as unknown with a route to finding out. A second error is treating a broker-side “no” as confidential so as not to damage the relationship; a deferral the merchant does not understand will simply be re-attempted elsewhere with the same file.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: write two letters for one declined file — the merchant-facing explanation and the note you keep on file. The merchant letter must state whose decision it was, quote the reason as given, offer the request route with its deadline and the office to contact if reasons were absent or insufficient, and list what next steps are and are not available. Model response: the letter contains no promise about a future outcome, no invented reason and no reference to speed or likelihood. Self-review rubric: check for three prohibited phrasings — a guaranty of approval, an implication of influence over a funder, and a fee described without reference to work performed — and for one required element, the sixty-day request window where it applies.
depth.summary: A decline is a communication problem with legal content attached, and most of the value is created or destroyed in the explanation rather than in the decision. Establish whose decision it is, use the funder's own words, know which business-credit notification track the file is on, and convert the outcome into either a specific reason the merchant can act on or an honest statement that the reason is not yet known. The transferable habit is refusing to be the source of a reason no document supports, and pricing the alternative: one written request against about $420 and six hours of blindly re-applying.

lessons.title: Re-application timing: what actually changes an outcome, and what merely repeats one
lessons.explanation: Merchants are usually told to re-apply “when things look better.” That instruction is useless because it does not identify a variable. There are exactly five categories of change that move a funding decision, and everything else is noise. The first is a reduced existing obligation: a balance paid down changes both the headroom available and the amount the funder can advance against the same receipts. The second is new or better evidence of receipts: two more months of statements, a processor settlement report, a filed tax return, or a signed contract with deliveries dated in the period. Evidence changes a projection into a measurement. The third is elapsed time itself, where a program has a minimum tenure or a minimum operating history requirement; time is a variable that cannot be accelerated honestly. The fourth is a corrected record: a disputed account that a consumer reporting agency reinvestigates and deletes or updates, a judgment that is satisfied and released, a tax lien with a recorded payoff, or a financing statement that should have been terminated and was. The fifth is a resolved eligibility condition, which is the status-based case from the previous lesson. What does not change an outcome: a different broker with the same file, a new application with no new evidence, an additional inquiry, and a verbal assurance that things have improved. Two mechanical points are worth knowing precisely. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, when a consumer disputes the completeness or accuracy of an item directly with a consumer reporting agency, the agency must conduct a reasonable reinvestigation free of charge and complete it within thirty days, extendable by no more than fifteen additional days in the circumstances the statute describes. So a correction has a roughly month-scale timeline, not a same-week one. And under Uniform Commercial Code Article 9 a financing statement remains effective for five years from filing, with continuation possible only if filed within the six months before expiration; a paid-off advance does not clear the record by itself. Re-application timing is therefore arithmetic with dates attached, not patience.
lessons.example: Terrence operates a mobile detailing business with $41,000 in monthly deposits, or $9,461.54 a week, and a contribution margin of 40 percent, which is $3,784.62 a week. He carries an advance with nine weeks of remittances left: $23,400 remaining at $1,300 a week. He wants $30,000 more for a second van and a water-reclamation system. Option one, apply now. A $30,000 net advance at a factor of 1.30 repays $39,000 over 26 weeks, which is $1,500 a week. Combined remittances are $1,300 + $1,500 = $2,800 a week, or 29.59 percent of weekly receipts, and they consume $2,800 of $3,784.62 of weekly contribution, which is 73.98 percent. Coverage — contribution divided by remittances — is 1.35. That is not automatically fatal, but note the timing: for the first ten weeks the combined load sits above a quarter of receipts, and only from week eleven, when the old advance is fully retired, does the load fall to $1,500, or 15.85 percent. Ten of the twenty-six weeks in the new term, 38.46 percent, are carried at the higher combined rate. Option two, wait eight weeks. The old balance falls by 8 × $1,300 = $10,400 to $13,000, which leaves ten weeks rather than eighteen on the existing schedule. Nothing else changes and coverage improves: the same $2,800 combined load now lasts ten weeks instead of eighteen, and the remaining sixteen weeks carry $1,500 alone, which is 15.85 percent of receipts. If in the same eight weeks his deposits rise six percent, as they did in the equivalent period last year, weekly receipts become $10,029.23 and coverage at the same structure is 1.43. Read the two options together and the honest advice is specific: waiting eight weeks does not change the business's eligibility, it changes the number of weeks the file is carried at a strained combined load, from ten of twenty-six to zero, because the strain is now resolved before the new schedule starts.
lessons.question: A merchant wants a second advance now while her existing advance has eighteen weeks left at $1,300 a week. What is the strongest reason to consider waiting?
lessons.answer: Waiting moves the strained combined-remittance weeks out of the new term entirely: the same structure that carries ten of twenty-six weeks above a quarter of receipts today would carry none of them eight weeks later.
lessons.distractor: Waiting improves her credit score, and most funders use a minimum score as their first screen.
lessons.correction: The advisor cannot know a score will improve, and a credit score is not the variable that changed in this example; the paid-down balance is. The measurable difference is the overlap. With eighteen weeks of $1,300 remaining, the first ten weeks of a new twenty-six-week term carry $2,800 a week, and only after that does the load fall to $1,500. Deferring eight weeks removes the overlap, and if receipts grow as they did in the prior period, coverage at the same structure rises from 1.35 to 1.43. Claiming a score improvement would be a guess presented as a reason.

depth.definitions: Re-application is a new request, with its own evidence and its own decision, not a continuation of the prior one. A qualifying variable is a fact that a specific program's criteria measure. Elapsed tenure is time in business measured to a program's minimum. A reinvestigation is a consumer reporting agency's statutory re-examination of a disputed item. A termination statement is a filing that removes a financing statement from the record; a continuation is a filing that extends its effectiveness. Combined load is the sum of all remittances and scheduled debt service measured against receipts and against contribution. Overlap is the interval during which an existing obligation and a proposed new one run concurrently.
depth.mechanism: The mechanics here are what separate advice from encouragement. A funder's headroom calculation is subtraction: receipts less every existing and proposed debit. Adding a second obligation while the first still runs does not create new receipts; it consumes the same ones twice, which is why the overlap interval rather than the total term drives the strain. Deferring an application changes nothing about the business and everything about the overlap, because the first obligation's remaining balance is a function of time — $23,400 divided by $1,300 is eighteen weeks, and eight weeks later the balance is $13,000, which is ten weeks. Two statutory clocks run alongside this arithmetic. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act a dispute filed directly with a consumer reporting agency requires a reasonable reinvestigation completed within thirty days, with an extension of not more than fifteen additional days when the consumer supplies relevant information during that period, so a corrected record is a month-scale project. Under Article 9 a financing statement stays effective for five years, and a paid-off advance leaves the public record unchanged until a termination statement is filed — which the debtor can compel by authenticated demand, with a twenty-day compliance period. An advisor who says “give it a month and try again” is describing both clocks badly; an advisor who says “your balance reaches $13,000 in eight weeks, and file the demand letter this week so the old filing is off the record by then” is describing them well.
depth.secondExample: Now the mirror case, where waiting is the wrong advice. A dental practice with $96,000 in monthly deposits and no existing advances is declined for insufficient tenure: the practice is fourteen months old and the program requires twenty-four. Waiting ten months is the only route to that program, but it is not the only route to funding, and the practice has a dated use — a CBCT imaging unit with a quoted price that expires on a supplier's stated date. The correct answer is to re-route rather than to wait: a shorter-duration product with a different tenure threshold, a lease or equipment structure against the asset being purchased, or a smaller amount sourced from an intermediary lender. Note the transferable rule: a re-application question is always “which variable does this specific program measure, and is that variable the binding constraint?” When the binding constraint is a program rule and another program does not share it, waiting is a cost with no benefit. When the binding constraint is the merchant's own balance sheet, waiting is the cheapest fix available and should be priced as such.
depth.mistake: The classic error is treating an additional application as a change in the file. It is not. A second submission with the same evidence, the same obligations and the same reasons produces the same decision and adds inquiries and record entries. The diagnostic test is one sentence: name the variable that changed since the last decision, and name the document that shows it. If the sentence cannot be completed, the file is not ready. A second error is the opposite: waiting when the binding constraint belongs to one program rather than to the business, which converts a routing question into a lost quarter. Learners often conflate the two because both feel like “patience”.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: take a file with an existing obligation and a proposed new one and build a two-column week-by-week table for twenty-six weeks showing combined remittances, combined remittances as a share of weekly receipts, and coverage. Then repeat it with the application deferred by the number of weeks needed to retire the existing obligation. Model response: a strong answer identifies the exact week in which the overlap ends, states coverage at its lowest point in each scenario, and finishes with one sentence naming the variable that would change between now and the later date. Self-review rubric: any table that omits either the receipts share or the coverage figure is incomplete, and any recommendation that does not name a changeable, documentable variable is encouragement rather than analysis.
depth.summary: Re-application is an arithmetic question about variables and dates, not a waiting game. Five things move a decision: a reduced obligation, better evidence of receipts, elapsed tenure where a program measures it, a corrected record, and a resolved status condition. Deferral earns its keep only when it removes an overlap or closes a measured gap; when the binding constraint belongs to one program, the answer is to re-route instead. The exercised numbers give the shape of it: a combined load of $2,800 a week against $3,784.62 of contribution is coverage of 1.35 and consumes 73.98 percent, and deferring eight weeks removes the ten-week overlap entirely.

lessons.title: Stacking and its real costs: describing a second position honestly
lessons.explanation: Stacking means more than one advance or receivables purchase encumbering the same future receipts at the same time. The FTC's 2020 staff perspective on small business financing names it directly, describing business owners forced to renew advances or take several at once, potentially encumbering the same receipts, in order to meet repayment obligations and avoid shutting down. The definition is mechanical rather than moral: a second position does not create new receipts, so it divides receipts that are already claimed. What follows from that is a set of costs that are easy to state and hard to feel, which is why merchants need them stated. The first cost is the payment load itself. A file with $2,250 a week already committed that takes on another $1,642.86 a week has $3,892.86 of fixed weekly claims where it previously had $2,250. The second cost is the loss of shock absorption. A fixed schedule does not fall when sales fall, so a business at 33.74 percent of receipts can be at 39.69 percent after a fifteen percent sales decline, with the same dollars due. The third cost is the reconciliation problem. Where the agreement provides for a true-up or reconciliation — and under structures such as Virginia's sales-based financing definition, a fixed-payment agreement with a reconciliation that adjusts the payment to a percentage of sales is itself a form of sales-based financing — the promised adjustment depends on evidence that both positions now claim. Two secured parties reconciling against one receipts base produces disputes about which one gets adjusted first. The fourth cost is priority. A later filing does not displace an earlier one; perfection under Article 9 turns on filing and, for purchase-money claims, on timing relative to the debtor's receipt of the collateral, so a merchant who believes a new advance has replaced an old one may find both claims live on the record. The fifth cost is the deadline pressure a stacked file creates, which is where manufactured urgency and real urgency get confused. None of this means a second position is never correct. It means the merchant is entitled to the arithmetic before the decision, and the advisor is obliged to disclose that a second position is what is being proposed.
lessons.example: Cornerstone Fitness carries an advance with 12 of 24 weeks elapsed: original net $40,000 at a factor of 1.35, so a $54,000 repayment at $2,250 a week, of which $27,000 remains. The owner asks for $25,000 more for equipment the landlord will not finance. He has been told by another broker that “the payments overlap, so nothing really changes.” Run the numbers. The new advance nets $25,000 at a factor of 1.38, which repays $34,500 over 21 weeks, or $1,642.86 a week. Combined weekly remittances are $2,250 + $1,642.86 = $3,892.86. Against weekly receipts of $600,000 ÷ 52 = $11,538.46, that is 33.74 percent. At a 35 percent contribution margin, weekly contribution is $4,038.46, so the combined remittances consume $3,892.86 of $4,038.46, which is 96.39 percent of contribution; coverage is 1.04. That is the figure that answers the “nothing really changes” claim: 96.39 percent of the business's weekly contribution is now committed before rent, payroll or any other fixed cost is paid from it. Add one realistic shock. If receipts fall fifteen percent, as they did in the merchant's own off-season, weekly receipts become $11,538.46 × 0.85 = $9,807.69 and the fixed remittances are 39.69 percent of receipts. Contribution falls to $3,432.69 and coverage falls to 0.88, meaning the two remittances exceed weekly contribution by $460.16, before any other obligation. And price the new money honestly: the new $25,000 net costs $34,500 in repayment, which is $138 per $100 of net proceeds, disclosed as that figure and as a weekly remittance amount — not as an interest rate, because a factor is not an interest rate and commercial financing is generally not subject to the Truth in Lending Act's annual-percentage-rate disclosure requirement for personal credit.
lessons.question: A merchant with $27,000 remaining on an existing advance wants a second advance now. He says the payments overlap so nothing changes. Which correction is strongest?
lessons.answer: The overlap is the change: combined remittances become $3,892.86 a week, which is 33.74 percent of receipts and 96.39 percent of weekly contribution, and a fifteen percent sales decline would push that to 39.69 percent with coverage falling to 0.88.
lessons.distractor: Nothing substantial changes as long as the second advance is repaid over a shorter term than the first, because the total repayment amount is what matters.
lessons.correction: Term length does not reduce the overlap; it determines how long it lasts. What matters at any given week is the sum of the fixed claims against the same receipts, which the example puts at 96.39 percent of contribution and coverage of 1.04 before any shock. Choosing a shorter term raises the weekly figure and lengthens nothing, so it makes the peak load worse, not better.

depth.definitions: A first position is an obligation with the earliest claim on the pledged receipts; a second position follows it. Stacking is the presence of more than one advance or receivables purchase against the same receipts at the same time. Contribution is receipts less variable costs, and coverage is contribution divided by scheduled remittances. A fixed schedule is a remittance that does not vary with sales; a share-of-receipts or true-up structure adjusts the amount to a percentage of sales or revenue. Shock absorption is the capacity to absorb a decline in receipts without failing to meet obligations. Per-hundred cost is the repayment amount divided by net proceeds, expressed as dollars per $100.
depth.mechanism: Two properties make stacking behave differently from an ordinary additional obligation. The first is that receipts are a shared base: obligations are fixed in dollars while receipts vary, so combining obligations converts a variable revenue stream into a larger fixed claim, and each added dollar of fixed claim consumes a larger share of contribution without adding any receipts. That is why coverage, not the amount borrowed, is the number that predicts difficulty. The second property is documentary and public. Under Article 9 a financing statement must be filed to perfect a security interest as a general rule, and it remains effective for five years unless continued within the six months before expiration, so an obligation that has been repaid can still appear on the record and can still be claimed against until a termination statement is filed. A merchant who takes a second position on the understanding that the first is finished may therefore be stacking against a live filing. The sales-based financing statutes add a third layer in the states that have them: where the law defines sales-based financing to include a fixed payment with a true-up reconciliation, the promise to adjust payments becomes part of the regulated disclosure, and the reconciliation evidence has to be produced by someone. In a stacked file, two parties are asking for the same evidence.
depth.secondExample: A contrasting stacked file is genuinely defensible, and the difference is measurable rather than stylistic. A commercial laundry takes a $60,000 first position in March for a boiler replacement, and in July a $22,000 second position at a factor of 1.25 — $27,500 over 20 weeks, or $1,375 a week — to fund a route-expansion contract that is already signed, with deliveries dated from August and a stated contribution per delivery. Weekly receipts before the second advance are $18,000 and the existing remittance is $1,600, so 8.89 percent of receipts. Adding $1,375 takes the total to $2,975, or 16.53 percent of receipts. At a 38 percent margin, contribution is $6,840 and coverage is 2.30, so the shock case at a fifteen percent decline still leaves receipts of $15,300, contribution of $5,814 and coverage of 1.95. The features that make this file different are not enthusiasm: the use is contracted rather than hoped for, the second position is smaller relative to receipts, the coverage has a wide margin in the shock case, and both positions are disclosed in writing to the merchant with their per-hundred cost. Stacking is not a synonym for bad; it is a change in the structure of the claims, and the test is whether the arithmetic survives a decline.
depth.mistake: The recurring error is treating stacking as a permission question rather than an arithmetic one: “will the second funder allow it?” The correction is to state coverage under the combined load and under a decline before the question of permission arises, because a funder that permits stacking is not thereby making it survivable. A second, related error is using a shorter term to make the second advance look light. A shorter term raises the weekly remittance and shortens the overlap window, which concentrates the strain rather than removing it. A third error is describing the new money without disclosing that a second position is being created at all; if the merchant does not know there will be two claims on one receipts base, the merchant has not consented to the structure.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: for a stacked proposal, build a one-page disclosure with four lines — existing weekly remittance and remaining weeks, proposed weekly remittance and term, combined remittance as a share of receipts and of contribution, and combined remittance as a share of receipts and coverage after a fifteen percent decline. Model response: the page names both filing dates if known, states the per-hundred cost of each position, and closes with the single coverage figure at which the file stops working in the merchant's own season. Self-review rubric: a correct page contains no rate, no annualised figure, no “nothing changes” language, and no recommendation that is unconditional on the declared shock case.
depth.summary: Stacking is best understood as a change in the structure of claims rather than a category of misconduct: the same receipts carry more fixed dollars, shock absorption falls, reconciliation becomes contested, and filings persist until terminated. The exercised figures put the difference in plain sight — combined remittances at 33.74 percent of receipts and 96.39 percent of contribution, coverage of 1.04, and coverage of 0.88 after a fifteen percent decline. The correct sequence is arithmetic first, disclosure second, decision third, and permission from a funder somewhere after that.

questions.prompt: A harvester with 11 months of operating history, two open advances and three of the twelve statement months supplied asks you to “just submit it and see.” What is the defensible action?
questions.answer: Run the screen, write a dated note naming the tenure gap, the two open obligations and the missing months as the blocking items, and state the amount the supplied evidence supports instead of submitting.
questions.distractor: Submit the application because a decision is faster than a document request and the funder may weigh the file differently than you do.
questions.correction: Submitting first moves the evidence check downstream, where the outcome is usually a documentation-driven decline that teaches the merchant nothing. The screen costs about an hour and a half of review against the merchant's hours, statement fees and any non-refundable processing fee, and it produces the number the file can actually support. Note also the two-sided question: nothing here suggests the merchant should be meeting a new fixed obligation in month eleven at all, which is a separate conclusion from fundability.

questions.prompt: A file has no UCC or lien search on record, tax transcripts unrequested, and four of twelve statement months outstanding. How should these be classified and routed?
questions.answer: Documentation-only gaps: they close with searches, transcript orders and statements, involve no payment, and should be ordered this week while any substantive conditions are being worked.
questions.distractor: Fixable conditions requiring payoff arrangements, so the merchant should be given an amount and a payment schedule for each one.
questions.correction: Nothing here requires money to change hands, so treating them as payoff conditions would invent obligations and delay the file for no reason. Documentation-only items are the advisor's own work product; the merchant's job is to authorise access or supply the statements. Keep the columns separate: a condition misrouted into the fixable column becomes a paid delay, and one misrouted into the permanent column becomes a needless decline.

questions.prompt: A funder notifies a merchant of a decline with the single sentence that the file “did not achieve a qualifying score on our credit scoring system.” The merchant's revenue is $2.2 million. What does the regulation require and what should you do?
questions.answer: Tell the merchant the stated reason is expressly insufficient and that a written statement of specific reasons may be requested under the larger-business track, with the request addressed to the creditor within the statutory window.
questions.distractor: Tell the merchant the reason is sufficient because scoring systems are protected and the funder is not obliged to explain them.
questions.correction: The regulation states that a reference to a qualifying score on the creditor's own system, or to internal standards, is not a sufficient statement of specific reasons. For a business above the $1 million gross-revenue line the creditor must notify of the action taken within a reasonable time and provide written reasons on the applicant's written request made within sixty days of that notification. The advisor's role is to relay that route accurately, not to accept the inadequate reason on the merchant's behalf.

questions.prompt: A merchant's existing advance has eighteen weeks left at $1,300 a week and she wants a new $30,000 facility now. What is the strongest argument for deferring eight weeks?
questions.answer: Deferral removes the overlap: the eight-week wait cuts the old balance from $23,400 to $13,000, so the ten weeks in which combined remittances run at 29.59 percent of receipts disappear from the new term entirely.
questions.distractor: Deferral improves the credit score, which is the first screen most funders apply to a file of this size.
questions.correction: The credit-score claim is a guess, and a score is not the variable that changes here. The measurable variable is the remaining balance: $23,400 ÷ $1,300 = eighteen weeks, so eight weeks later the balance is $13,000 and the concurrent-load interval shortens from ten weeks of the new twenty-six-week term to none. Coverage at the same structure moves from 1.35 to 1.43 if receipts grow as they did in the prior period.

questions.prompt: A merchant with $11,538.46 of weekly receipts and $4,038.46 of weekly contribution wants a $25,000 advance while an advance with $27,000 outstanding still runs at $2,250 a week. What figure settles the “nothing really changes” claim?
questions.answer: The combined load: $2,250 plus a new $1,642.86 is $3,892.86 a week, or 96.39 percent of weekly contribution with coverage of 1.04, and coverage falls to 0.88 with a $460.16 weekly shortfall after a fifteen percent sales decline.
questions.distractor: The total repayment amount of the new advance alone, since overlapping payments are separate obligations and each should be judged on its own term.
questions.correction: Each obligation is real, but they compete for the same receipts and the same contribution, so the combined figure is what determines survivability. Judging the new advance alone hides the fact that 96.39 percent of weekly contribution is committed before any other cost is paid and that a single bad month produces a shortfall. Note also that the new money is priced as $34,500 of repayment on $25,000 of net proceeds, which is $138 per $100 of net and is not an interest rate or an annual percentage rate.

units.title: Alternatives, fairness, records and the capstone file review

lessons.title: Alternative products and when a smaller amount is the better answer
lessons.explanation: A funding conversation that begins with an amount and ends with a product has the order backwards. The correct order is use, then duration, then source, then amount. Use determines what can be funded at all: under SBA's published terms, a 504 loan cannot be used for working capital or inventory, and cannot consolidate, repay or refinance debt that does not meet the definition of qualified debt in 13 CFR 120.882, paragraphs (e) and (g), which means a merchant who needs working capital is outside that program no matter how strong the file is. Duration follows from what is being financed: a five-year asset financed over twenty-six weeks is a mismatch in both directions, because it forces repayment faster than the asset produces cash and it leaves the merchant refinancing again later. Source is the part merchants rarely hear enumerated. SBA-guaranteed loans of up to $5 million in most cases, with SBA Express and Export Express delivery methods capped at $500,000; microloans of up to $50,000 made through specially designated intermediary lenders, with an average microloan of about $13,000 according to SBA's own program page, which is the right shape for a merchant who needs $15,000 rather than $50,000; equipment financing and leases secured by the asset itself; invoice financing or factoring against a specific receivable; a business line of credit where availability is drawn and repaid rather than advanced as a lump sum; and community lenders and intermediaries whose size limits are different from the mainstream. The amount is the last decision and it should be the smallest number that accomplishes the stated use, because every extra dollar of principal adds dollars of cost while adding nothing to the purpose. This is not a small point. A merchant who borrows $40,000 for an $18,000 purpose has bought $22,000 of unavoidable cost to hold cash it did not need, and if the extra sits idle the cost per hundred dollars of net proceeds applied to the actual use is worse than the headline figure suggests.
lessons.example: Ridgeline Landscaping needs $18,000 for a used enclosed trailer and a second mower, and asks for $40,000 because a broker suggested that the larger amount would “leave room.” Compare three answers. Right-sized advance: $18,000 net at a factor of 1.32 repays $23,760 over 24 weeks, which is $990 a week, and prices the money at $132 per $100 of net proceeds. Equipment term loan: $18,000 over 60 months at a 9.00 percent note rate gives a monthly payment of $373.65 and total payments of $22,419.02, which is $4,419.02 of interest and $124.55 per $100 of principal, and the schedule matches the life of the asset rather than running three times as fast. Oversized advance as requested: $40,000 net at a factor of 1.30 repays $52,000 over 26 weeks, which is $2,000 a week. The difference between the requested amount and the amount the use requires is $52,000 − $23,760 = $28,240 of additional repayment and $2,000 − $990 = $1,010 of additional weekly remittance, in exchange for $22,000 of cash that the stated use does not consume. Note what is not being compared. The term loan is not automatically better than the advance because its per-hundred figure is lower; the two instruments carry different obligations, different prepayment terms and different access to the asset financed. What is comparable is the use: both fund the trailer and the mower, and the advance's 24-week schedule finishes four years before the loan's. The decisive question is whether the $1,010 a week of extra remittance buys anything. For a use of $18,000 with a dated purpose, it does not. It displaces roughly two and a half weeks of the merchant's contribution margin every month for no operational benefit, and it makes the file harder to renew later. A fourth and simpler answer is available too: split the purchase. Buy the trailer now at $7,000 and the second mower in the spring when the seasonal contracts are signed, which removes the financing need for the second item almost entirely.
lessons.question: A merchant asks for $40,000 for an $18,000 equipment need and says the extra will “leave room.” Which response is the strongest?
lessons.answer: Size the financing to the $18,000 use and show the arithmetic: $23,760 repayment at $990 a week and $132 per $100 of net, against $52,000 repayment at $2,000 a week if the full amount is taken.
lessons.distractor: Take the $40,000 because the merchant can always pay down the excess early, and the extra cash is a safety buffer against a slow month.
lessons.correction: Early payoff is a contractual question, not an assumption: the agreement's prepayment terms govern whether paying down the excess actually reduces cost, and under a purchase of receivables the purchased amount is generally payable as agreed regardless of how quickly receipts arrive. So the buffer is not free — it costs $28,240 of additional repayment and $1,010 a week. Where a buffer is genuinely needed, the honest instrument is a line of credit whose availability is drawn and repaid, not a lump-sum advance held against future uncertainty.

depth.definitions: Right-sizing is choosing the smallest amount that accomplishes a stated, dated use. Match of duration to use is selecting a repayment schedule consistent with the period over which the funded asset or activity produces cash. A microloan is an SBA-program loan of up to $50,000 made through a designated intermediary lender; SBA's program page states the maximum and describes the average loan size. A 504 loan is a long-term, fixed-asset program delivered through Certified Development Companies, with a statutory list of eligible uses. An SBA Express or Export Express delivery method carries a lower maximum than the general 7(a) program. Net proceeds are the amount disbursed to the merchant after fees deducted or withheld at disbursement, and they are the correct denominator for any per-hundred cost figure.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism that makes right-sizing rational is marginal rather than moral. Each additional dollar of principal carries a cost that is fixed at the outset, while its benefit depends entirely on whether it funds something productive. In a factor structure, the repayment amount rises proportionally with the purchased amount, so the marginal dollar is priced exactly like the first dollar and brings no volume discount in cost terms. In an interest-bearing loan the marginal dollar is cheaper in per-dollar terms because the fixed cost of originating the loan is already covered, which is why adding a small amount to an already-existing facility is different from taking a larger advance. The second mechanism is duration. Financing a five-year asset over six months concentrates the entire cost into the first season of the asset's life; if the season underperforms, the obligation is already behind the asset's earning pattern. The third mechanism is the buffer question, and the answer is structural rather than arithmetic: a buffer is a liquidity need, and the instruments that serve liquidity needs are lines of credit and reserves, whose cost is incurred only when used. A lump-sum advance held as a buffer incurs its full cost whether or not the buffer is ever drawn upon.
depth.secondExample: A different file shows when the larger amount is the better answer, and the reason is not the balance sheet. A specialty grocer with $210,000 of monthly receipts and no existing obligations is offered a $60,000 advance at a factor of 1.38 or a $25,000 advance at a factor of 1.25. The use is a dated inventory build for a holiday season that runs eight weeks at roughly three times normal weekly volume. The smaller amount carries a lower per-hundred cost — $125 against $138 — but it does not fund the inventory, which would force a second, later advance at a worse time and add a second filing. Here the larger amount is the right answer because it matches a real, dated, dollar-quantified use. The general rule survives the counterexample: right-size to the use, not to the smallest number available. What changes is the use, which on this file is genuinely $60,000 and on the previous file was genuinely $18,000. The mistake is not choosing a large amount; it is choosing an amount no use supports, and the way to avoid it is to make the merchant write the use down with a dollar figure and a date before any amount is quoted.
depth.mistake: The most common error is treating the approved amount as a measure of success, so that a $40,000 approval is preferable to an $18,000 approval on the same use. The correction is to convert the difference into a weekly figure the merchant recognises: $1,010 a week, or roughly two and a half weeks of contribution margin per month in the worked example. A companion error is assuming the extra amount can simply be returned early; that assumption depends on contract terms that must be read rather than assumed, and in a purchase of receivables the purchased amount is generally payable as agreed. A third error is recommending a product whose eligible uses exclude the merchant's need — working capital or inventory against a 504 program, for instance — because the headline terms looked attractive before the use list was checked.
depth.application: Nonblocking task: for one merchant, write the use down in a single sentence with a dollar figure, a date and a consequence of delay; then list every source you can name with its size limit and whether the stated use fits the program's eligible uses. Model response: a strong answer contains at least three named sources with their actual limits, at least one answer that costs nothing (defer the purchase, split it, or negotiate terms with the supplier), and a financing amount that equals the use rather than the approved maximum. Self-review rubric: no amount may appear in the answer before the use sentence does, and every product named must be accompanied by an eligible-use statement.
depth.summary: Order the conversation use, duration, source, amount, and the amount becomes almost mechanical. Programs have eligible-use lists that can exclude a merchant outright — a 504 loan cannot fund working capital or inventory — while microloans up to $50,000 with an average around $13,000, equipment financing, lines of credit and invoice facilities each suit a different shape of need. Right-sizing is not austerity: in the contrasting file the larger amount was correct because a dated, quantified use supported it, while in the original file $22,000 of additional principal bought no operational benefit and cost $28,240 of additional repayment.
